newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil poised to rule on contested Indian lands.
newsitem.headline: Brazil poised to rule on contested Indian lands.

text.p: Brazil's government was due to consider the fate of several Indian territories, which rights groups fear could mean a sharp cut in the size of at least one indigenous reserve, officials said on Wednesday.

A spokesman said Justice Minister Nelson Jobim would fly on Thursday to the Raposa/Serra do Sol reserve in Roraima state, the first of eight territories he must rule on under a new law allowing non-Indians to challenge indigenous lands.
There, on the remote rainforest frontier with Guyana, he will take stock of invasions by wildcat gold miners and Indian claims that farmers were trying to drive them off their land.

"The minister has to decide whether to demarcate the Raposa/Serra do Sol territory and will spend two days flying over the reserve in a helicopter to monitor invasions," the Justice Ministry spokesman said.
Rights groups said they were concerned Jobim would reduce the land the 11,000 Indians of the Makuxi, Ingariko, Wapixana, Taurepang and Patamona tribes in Raposa consider their own.
The demarcation battle caps 20 years of confrontation in Raposa. "The situation is very tense," said Fany Ricardo of independent pressure group Instituto Socioambiental.

Of a total of about 556 Indian areas in Brazil, 83 faced legal challenges after Jobim pushed through the law this year allowing non-Indians to lodge claims against indigenous territories. All but eight were found invalid or rejected.

But the Raposa situation is complicated by the existence of towns and because some farmers hold property rights, officials said. The towns would have to be evacuated and the farmers expelled if all the territory were to be recognised.

Concern about Jobim's most likely course of action has spread to Washington, where 17 members of the House of Representatives led by California Democrat Tom Lantos and Illinois Republican John Porter wrote Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso urging protection for the Indians.
"We are concerned that a reduction of this area will set a precedent for the possible reduction of other indigenous areas," they said this week, adding that they feared "severe violence will follow."
The Instituto Socioambiental said Raposa had a history of violence, with frequent invasions by "garimpeiros", as wildcat gold-diggers are known in Portuguese, and by cattle ranchers.

It also accused the state government of condoning "institutionalized violence" by local police against indigenous people, including "illegal imprisonment, destruction of property, assault and even murder".
